title: DHS Chief Defends Football Trip Amid Travel Chaos, Clashes With Lawmakers Over ICE Tactics
snippet: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin faced intense questioning on Capitol Hill, defending a personal trip to a college football game during widespread air travel disruptions and pushing back against lawmakers' concerns over recent technical outages and immigration enforcement.
content:
WASHINGTON — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin found himself on the defensive Wednesday during a fiery House Homeland Security Committee hearing, answering for a personal weekend trip to a college football game while air travel across the nation was paralyzed by a massive ground stop.

The standard annual oversight hearing quickly turned into a high-stakes interrogation. Beyond the flight disruptions, lawmakers pressed Mullin and top intelligence officials on a string of high-profile technical outages and raised sharp concerns about the vetting and training of thousands of newly hired federal immigration officers.

Defense of Football Trip Amid Flight Cancellations

Mullin faced heat over his decision to fly to Louisiana last Saturday to attend the LSU-Texas football game with family while thousands of stranded travelers were left scrambling at airports nationwide following a system-wide ground stop.

The DHS chief defended the excursion, emphasizing that the flight took place after the nationwide restriction was lifted and asserting that canceling the long-planned trip could have projected instability.

"If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly," Mullin testified, reiterating that he reimbursed the government for the mandatory use of official aircraft.

Addressing the underlying aviation crisis, Mullin stood by the administration's emergency response. Officials attributed the ground stop to newly installed routers overloading the Federal Aviation Administration's telecommunications infrastructure. Mullin highlighted that air traffic controllers safely landed more than 4,000 airborne flights without a single safety incident once the outage began.

Officials Dismiss Cyberattack Rumors

Alongside FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Mullin sought to quell growing public speculation that recent disruptions—including an hourslong Microsoft outage, banking glitches, an internal NSA network disruption, and the FAA ground stop—were the result of a coordinated cyberattack.

"I'm 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems," Mullin told committee members.

Clayton echoed those assurances, confirming that current intelligence points to separate technical maintenance issues rather than state-sponsored sabotage. However, the testimony unfolded as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), housed within DHS, continues to operate without a Senate-confirmed director following recent staffing reductions.

Tense Clashes Over ICE Training and Enforcement

Immigration policy sparked some of the hearing's most heated moments. Democratic lawmakers scrutinized U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) following an unprecedented hiring surge of 12,000 new officers and agents, questioning whether rushed background checks and shortened training contributed to recent fatal encounters.

Mullin insisted that all active ICE agents have passed complete background checks and that any officers who have not finished their mandatory 13-week training curriculum have been placed on administrative leave.

The session turned contentious when Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.) pressed Mullin on fatal officer-involved shootings, including high-profile deaths in Minneapolis. When McIver asked if he had regrets regarding the administration's aggressive deportation push, Mullin stated he had none.

"You are killing people," McIver stated during the exchange.

"No ma’am. That’s your opinion," Mullin responded before the committee moved on to further questioning.

Mullin, who assumed leadership of DHS following the departure of Kristi Noem earlier this year, remains a central figure as the administration navigates ongoing legislative friction and heightened public scrutiny over security, infrastructure, and border enforcement.
